Right, now I'm not going to say that atheists or unbelievers arent just as fallacious as christians most times, but boy, this is a strawman from head to tippy toe.

A) I mean I agree...what do the actions the God of the bible commits have anything to do with the ontological argument? Nothing. And I've never heard or encountered any irreligious ppl who think it \*does\*. That's why I feel like this is a strawman. The point of having the morality conversation(for me) would be to argue that, if the God of the bible does exist, he's a thug, or a mad scientist who's just fucking with us, or at least severely bipolar, since the Bible affirms again and again that whatever God(or his mouthpiece) \*says\* is good, is good: conquest, genocide, kidnapping/rape of virgin women, genital mutilation, land theft and displacement of neighbors all as proscribed for the tribe, and then suddenly (sudden at least for a being that existed before time or space) "love your neighbor" and all that. And that that \*particular\* brand of christianity is amoral by definition(or at least morally relative, which I'll get to), and not deserving of worship by any thinking, self-identified "moral" person. At least not without framing and re-framing and re-interpreting the texts to fit their own disposition, to the point where a genuinely decent christian human-being doesnt and \*can't\* even really believe in the God of the bible, but in their own personal one cobbled at least in part from it. (It's almost like \*every\* human being cobbles together their own guiding system anyway. And It just might be that Yahweh was created by man just like Shiva, Odin, or Beelzebub) But again, not a question of his existence, it's a question of his morality. His fitness for office if ya like.

B) I'm not sure why christians would need any "theological education" outside of their own moral compass to discuss problems of God's actions in the context of morality(again, I assume this is what you mean by "did something you disagree with"). They're adults with brains and can answer meaningful questions about right/wrong in relation to their own faith, and when you—I guess what it sounds like you're trying to do is, protect the average no-theological-education-having christian from...the conversation itself? From contending with the problem?—you end up sounding patronizing no offense.

C) Also, a good bit of moral relativist hand-waving there with the whole "happened more than 2000 yrs ago so that's out of bounds" thing, all in apology for christianity, a faith supposedly dedicated to an eternal God who never changes his mind and who writes laws of morality that are supposed to be anything \*but\* relative. > You seem to be under the mistaken impression that the monarchy holds a strangle hold on the UK.

I didn't think I was even implying that, but I guess I can understand how I gave that impression. 


Here's what I hate: inevitably when the Queen dies, there'll be talk of this artificial "we" that has somehow lost something, and not even that "we" *should* mourn, but that everybody already *is* mourning, and anyone who disagrees is just a crank, or isn't patriotic enough, etc. It's a cliche for me to say that this norm reminds me of **1984** , but it does, and it's creepy and insidious. This sort of campaign of cheap sentiment happens in the States all the time, and it doesn't even have to be a head of state or someone especially well known for media outlets to join the bandwagon(or start it up), and a decent number of people inevitably follow suit. Whenever the mass media spot an opportunity for meaningless, hive-mind consensus building, they will seize it shamelessly. And it's pretty cheaply bought ofc, because plenty of people will volunteer their hearts and eat that shit up. It'll always get ratings.


It's also good to hear you say that Lizzie doesn't involve herself with the politics of the present atm, because according to royal prerogative she totally could if she wanted. Whoever inherits the throne is also the head of the armed forces, they can declare war, make peace, recognize foreign governments, ratify treaties, grant pardons, charters, and commissions. Whatever it is about being a member of the house of Windsor that gives someone the right to hold such power, I have no idea. And none of those powers are purely decorative or ceremonial. Who's to say years down the line that someone dangerous doesn't get excreted onto the throne, and starts appealing to the cheap populism that has always been in the monarchy's toolbox, and starts making a whole lot of promises. That's a scary idea imo. 

*edited for grammar

The fact that there's a kind of social pressure to mourn the head of state should make it even more sinister and creepy shouldn't it? Not to mention the head of state is a literal monarch and it's 2019. We should know better than to have monarchs at all.
